title: Java Enterprise Architecture: The Collections Framework
description: The final frontier of the BSSE curriculum. A comprehensive masterclass on the Java Collections Framework, covering Lists, Sets, Maps, underlying memory data structures, and advanced iteration.

subtopics.title: The Unified Framework & Generics
subtopics.content: Before the Collections Framework, Java developers had to rely on rigid arrays or build custom data structures from scratch. The Java Collections Framework (JCF) is a standard library of dynamic data structures. To ensure data safety, these collections use 'Generics' (<T>), which forces the collection to only accept one specific type of Object.
subtopics.callout_text: Collections can ONLY store Objects, never primitives. You cannot create a `List<int>`. You must use their Object Wrapper classes, like `List<Integer>`, `List<Double>`, or `List<Boolean>`.
list_items: **Map:** Key-Value dictionary pairs (Does not inherit from Collection).

subtopics.title: ArrayList vs. LinkedList
subtopics.content: Both classes implement the `List` interface, meaning they have the exact same methods (`.add()`, `.remove()`, `.get()`). However, their underlying memory architecture is completely different. Choosing the wrong one will destroy your application's performance.
subtopics.callout_text: An `ArrayList` defaults to 10 slots. When you add the 11th item, it doesn't just grow. The JVM pauses, creates a brand new 15-slot array, copies all 10 old items over, and deletes the old array. This is an O(N) operation.
list_items: **Use ArrayList:** When you read data 90% of the time and write 10% of the time (Search engines).
**Use LinkedList:** When you are constantly adding and deleting data from the middle of the list (Music playlist queues).

subtopics.title: HashSet vs. TreeSet
subtopics.content: Sets are designed to prevent duplicate data. If you attempt to add an item that already exists, the Set simply ignores the operation. The two main enterprise Sets are `HashSet` (built for pure speed) and `TreeSet` (built for alphabetical/numerical sorting).
subtopics.callout_text: A `HashSet` achieves instantaneous O(1) lookups by converting your data into a math equation (a Hash Code). It uses this number as a direct memory address, allowing the CPU to instantly verify if an item exists without scanning the whole list.
list_items: Cannot access items by an index number (`set.get(0)` does not exist).
If you need sorted data: Use `TreeSet`.

subtopics.title: HashMap Architecture
subtopics.content: A Map stores data in pairs. The 'Key' acts like a unique ID, and the 'Value' is the data attached to it. Just like Sets, you have `HashMap` (fast, random order) and `TreeMap` (slower, sorted by Key).
subtopics.callout_text: What happens if two different Keys generate the exact same Hash Code? Java handles this 'Collision' by storing both Key-Value pairs in the same memory bucket using a mini-LinkedList. It then uses the `.equals()` method to find the exact one you want.
list_items: Keys MUST be unique. Values can be duplicates.
Allows exactly one `null` Key, and multiple `null` Values.

subtopics.title: The Iterator & Fail-Fast Mechanics
subtopics.content: While you can use an Enhanced For-Loop (`for (String item : list)`) to read collections, you CANNOT use it to delete items. If you try to remove an item from a list while looping through it, Java throws a `ConcurrentModificationException`. To safely remove items during a loop, you must use an `Iterator`.
subtopics.callout_text: Because Maps have two elements (Keys and Values), you can't loop them normally. The most efficient way is to extract both simultaneously using `.entrySet()`: `for (Map.Entry<Integer, String> row : students.entrySet())`
list_items: **Comparable:** Modifies the class itself to give it a default sorting rule (e.g., sort Students by ID).
**Comparator:** An external tool used to create custom sorting rules on the fly (e.g., sort Students by Grade, then by Name).

sections.title: Java Systems Architecture: Exception Handling
sections.description: Master the JVM's error handling mechanics. Learn the Throwable hierarchy, propagation through the Call Stack, and how to engineer resilient, crash-proof enterprise software.

sections.title: Module 1: The Error Taxonomy & Throwable Hierarchy

subtopics.title: The 3 Types of Software Errors
subtopics.content:
Software engineers must anticipate and defend against three distinct categories of failure:

1. Compile-Time Errors: Syntax mistakes (missing semicolons, misspelled keywords). The code refuses to compile.
2. Logical Errors: The code compiles and runs, but the math or business logic is flawed (e.g., subtracting instead of adding).
3. Runtime Errors: The code is syntactically perfect, but an unexpected external event (like a missing file or a user typing text instead of a number) causes the JVM to crash during execution.
subtopics.callout_text: Exception Handling is strictly designed to manage Runtime Errors. You cannot 'catch' a syntax error, and you cannot 'catch' bad math. You only catch unpredictable runtime events.

subtopics.title: The Throwable Hierarchy
subtopics.content:
In Java, every error is an Object. At the very top of the architecture is the `Throwable` class. It splits into two massive branches:

1. Error: Catastrophic hardware/JVM failures (e.g., `OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError`). You should NEVER try to catch these. Let the program die.
2. Exception: Software-level issues that a good program should catch and recover from (e.g., `IOException`, `ArithmeticException`).
list_items: **Checked Exceptions:** (e.g., `IOException`). The compiler FORCES you to handle these before it even lets you run the code. They represent external threats outside your control.

**Unchecked Exceptions:** (e.g., `RuntimeException`, `NullPointerException`). The compiler ignores these. They usually represent poor programming (like dividing by zero) that you should fix with an `if` statement, not a try/catch block.

subtopics.title: The Defense Perimeter (Try/Catch)
subtopics.content: When a dangerous operation is about to occur, you wrap it in a `try` block. If the JVM detects a fatal error inside that block, it immediately halts execution and 'throws' an Exception object. The `catch` block acts as a safety net, catching the object and executing a backup plan without crashing the software.
subtopics.callout_text: You can have multiple catch blocks to handle different errors. But remember the Golden Rule of Polymorphism: Always catch the most specific exceptions first, and the generic `Exception` last!

subtopics.title: The Absolute Guarantee (Finally)
subtopics.content: The `finally` block is attached to the end of a try/catch structure. The code inside the `finally` block is mathematically guaranteed to execute, regardless of whether an error occurred, whether it was caught, or even if the method has a `return` statement inside the try block.
list_items: The `finally` block will run no matter what, UNLESS you explicitly kill the JVM memory process by calling `System.exit(0)` before it gets there.

subtopics.title: Throwing and Ducking (throws)
subtopics.content: Sometimes, a method doesn't want to handle an error. Instead, it uses the `throws` keyword in its signature to 'duck' and pass the responsibility up to whoever called it. This is called Exception Propagation. If no method catches the exception, it bubbles all the way up to the `main` method, crashing the program.
subtopics.callout_text: `throw` (singular) is an action verb used INSIDE the method to physically launch an error object. `throws` (plural) is a warning label attached to the method SIGNATURE.

subtopics.title: Engineering Custom Exceptions
subtopics.content: Enterprise applications often need errors specific to their business logic (e.g., `InsufficientFundsException` for a bank). You can create your own exception by inheriting from the `Exception` class.
